question: According to the manual, riding across which of the following increases your chance of falling or being involved in a crash?
choice_b: Uneven or slippery surfaces, railroad tracks, and grooves or gratings
choice_c: None of these surfaces present any added risk
choice_d: Only surfaces marked with a speed limit sign
explanation: Your chance of falling or being involved in a crash increases whenever you ride across uneven surfaces or obstacles, slippery surfaces, railroad tracks, and grooves and gratings.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.31-32, 'Handling Dangerous Surfaces'

question: If you must ride over a smaller obstacle, at approximately what angle should you approach it?
choice_b: Angle does not matter for obstacles
choice_c: As close to a 90-degree angle as possible
explanation: Try to avoid obstacles by slowing or going around them; if you must go over a smaller obstacle, approach it at as close to a 90-degree angle as possible and look where you want to go.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: When riding over an unavoidable obstacle, what body position technique does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Sit down as hard as possible on the seat
choice_b: Stand fully upright on the footrests with locked knees
choice_c: Lie flat against the fuel tank
choice_d: Rise slightly off the seat with weight on the footrests to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows
explanation: If you have to ride over the obstacle, slow down as much as possible before contact, make sure the motorcycle is straight, and rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: After riding over an object on the street, what should you do before continuing?
choice_a: Pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther
choice_b: Continue riding at normal speed with no inspection
choice_c: Immediately accelerate to test the tires
choice_d: Only check the tires once you arrive at your final destination
explanation: If you ride over an object on the street, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: Which of the following is identified in the manual as a surface that provides poor traction?
choice_a: Dry, clean asphalt in direct sunlight
choice_b: Wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road
explanation: Surfaces that provide poor traction include wet pavement (particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes away), gravel roads, mud, leaves, snow, ice, and wet lane markings or steel plates.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: What does the manual recommend to ride safely on slippery surfaces?
choice_a: Increase speed to get through the slippery section faster
choice_b: Make sudden, decisive movements to break through the slick spot
choice_c: Reduce speed, avoid sudden moves, and use both brakes gently
choice_d: Use only the rear brake and avoid the front brake entirely
explanation: To ride safely on slippery surfaces: reduce speed before you get to the slippery surface, avoid sudden moves (any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid), and use both brakes with gentle, gradual pressure.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: When it starts to rain, where does the manual recommend riding within the lane?
choice_a: In the exact center of the lane at all times
choice_b: As far right in the lane as possible, regardless of conditions
choice_c: It makes no difference; lane position is irrelevant in rain
choice_d: In the tire tracks left by vehicles, often the left tire track depending on traffic and conditions
explanation: The center of a lane can be hazardous when wet; when it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles -- often the left tire track will be the best position, depending on traffic and other roadway conditions.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Where do patches of ice tend to develop even after most of a road has cleared?
choice_a: In low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses
choice_b: Only in the exact center of the traffic lane
choice_c: Ice never persists once the sun rises
choice_d: Only on gravel roads, never on paved highways
explanation: Rain dries and snow melts faster on some sections of a road than others; patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: If a cautious rider cannot avoid riding on ice or snow, what should they do?
choice_a: Lean the motorcycle normally into any turns as usual
choice_b: Keep the motorcycle straight up, proceed as slowly as possible, stay off the brakes, and squeeze the clutch to coast if needed
choice_c: Brake hard immediately to slow down as quickly as possible
choice_d: Accelerate to maintain stability on the ice
explanation: Cautious riders avoid roads covered with ice or snow; if you can't, keep the motorcycle straight up and proceed as slowly as possible, staying off the brakes and squeezing the clutch to coast if you must travel at a walking pace.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.33, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: What is usually the safest way to cross railroad tracks that run perpendicular to your path?
choice_a: Always zigzag across the tracks at a shallow angle
choice_b: Stop directly on the tracks to check for trains
choice_c: Ride straight within your lane, since turning to take the tracks at a 90-degree angle can put you into another lane of traffic
choice_d: Cross diagonally at 45 degrees whenever possible
explanation: Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks; turning to take tracks at a 90-degree angle can be more dangerous because the direction may put you into another lane of traffic.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.33, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: For track and road seams that run parallel to your path, at what minimum angle should you cross them?
choice_c: Angle is irrelevant for parallel seams
choice_d: At least 45 degrees, making a deliberate turn so you're not thrown off balance
explanation: For track and road seams that run parallel to your path, move far enough away from tracks, ruts, or pavement seams to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn so you're not thrown off balance.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.33, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: What does the manual recommend when riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings that cause the motorcycle to weave?
choice_a: Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across rather than zigzagging
choice_b: Brake hard immediately to stop the weaving sensation
choice_c: Zigzag to compensate for the wandering feeling
choice_d: Accelerate sharply to punch through the grooves
explanation: Riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings may cause a motorcycle to weave; the uneasy, wandering feeling is generally not hazardous. Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across, since crossing at an angle forces riders to zigzag, which is far more hazardous.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.33-34, 'Grooves and Gratings'
